title: One Receptor Gene, Chosen in Steps

scenes.tts: A mouse olfactory neuron carries about a thousand odorant receptor genes. Yet a mature one transcribes just one gene, from just one copy. That is called singular choice. How does a cell make a choice that complete, and then keep it?
scenes.visual: Nucleus filled with receptor-gene tiles; one tile lights green and splits into two copies, one transcribed; a question mark over the grid
scenes.caption: A mouse olfactory neuron carries about a thousand odorant receptor genes. Yet a mature one transcribes just one gene, from just one copy. That is called singular choice. How does a cell make a choice that complete, and then keep it?

scenes.tts: Start with silence. Picture a library where nearly every book is chained shut, and one is left open. In mouse olfactory neurons, receptor genes carry repressive marks. These are marks of heterochromatin, which is tightly packed, silenced chromatin. The data suggest this silencing comes before any receptor expression can be detected.
scenes.visual: Red repressive marks land on nearly every gene tile, one stays open; heterochromatin chip; silencing arrow to expression detectable

scenes.tts: Now read one result carefully. In mouse neurons labelled for a receptor called P two, the active copy carried less of the marks than its inactive partner. So the chosen copy is less repressed. That is only a comparison. It does not show that the chosen gene silenced the others. The silencing was already there.

scenes.tts: How does one gene escape? An enhancer is a D N A element that raises the transcription of a gene it contacts. In mouse neurons, receptor gene clusters on eighteen chromosomes contact one another, in hubs. Single cell data indicate several competing hubs in developing neurons, before one gene dominates. The evidence supported a further step. Receptor R N A suppresses the competing receptors at a distance. The machinery for that is still unidentified.
scenes.visual: Chromosome capsules with gene and enhancer chips pull into three hubs; hubs pulse; one hub wins and makes receptor RNA with inhibitory arrows to the rivals
scenes.caption: How does one gene escape? An enhancer is a DNA element that raises the transcription of a gene it contacts. In mouse neurons, receptor gene clusters on 18 chromosomes contact one another, in hubs. Single-cell data indicate several competing hubs in developing neurons, before one gene dominates. The evidence supported a further step. Receptor RNA suppresses the competing receptors at a distance. The machinery for that is still unidentified.

scenes.tts: Next, the neuron must keep its choice. Receptor expression engages the unfolded protein response, the pathway by which a cell reacts to misfolded protein. In developing mouse neurons, a kinase called PERK acts first. Then a factor called A T F five promotes the gene for adenylyl cyclase three. That enzyme in turn relieves the stress. In young mice lacking it, lineage tracing showed more switching. So the feedback helps stabilize the choice.
scenes.visual: Chain from the chosen gene through PERK and ATF5 to Adcy3 with a feedback arrow back to the gene; lineage-tracing rows of marked cells with and without Adcy3

scenes.tts: Put it together. First comes silence. Then several hubs compete, and one gene dominates. Then feedback helps hold that choice in place. This mouse model is ordered but incomplete. Singular expression is the endpoint of a sequence. It is not a property of every stage.
